title: Okitsu citrus: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaTitle: Okitsu citrus: Fruit and Tree Characteristics
metaDescription: Okitsu citrus is a satsuma mandarin citrus variety from BPI Baguio (BNCRDC). See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: Okitsu citrus is a satsuma mandarin citrus variety, also sold or known as Okitsu (Satsuma mandarin) or Satsuma. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 2005 as NSIC 2005 Md 04. BPI Bncrdc bred it. Its record notes a yield of 10 kg/tree.

blocks.text: If you came here looking for Okitsu (Satsuma mandarin) or Satsuma, this is the same citrus. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry, with notes from its seller and farm sources. Compare it with the others in our [citrus variety finder](/crop-varieties/citrus), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [fertilizer for fruit trees](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. The mother tree of Okitsu was about 7 years old and about 1.5 meters tall when it was registered. Its record notes a yield of 10 kg/tree. It bears every year, with fruit in March August. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
The registry gives no pest or disease ratings for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.

The pests and diseases that hit citrus fields most often: [citrus greening](/diseases/citrus-greening), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug), [Oriental fruit fly](/pests/oriental-fruit-fly). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

A fruit of Okitsu weighs about 128 grams, and its shape is oblate. The flesh is orange and soft. Its sweetness measured 10.53 degrees Brix, the share of sugar in the juice. Most table fruit tastes sweet from about 12 Brix up. The edible part is 81.04 percent of the fruit. The registry notes its fruiting season as March August, bearing annual.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Small, flat, about 128 g, green yellow peel, juicy orange flesh, about 10.5 Brix.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: the satsuma in BPI Baguio's registered mandarin set, with the highest edible share (about 81 percent). Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant Okitsu citrus

Sweet oranges and mandarins grow best in the cooler, drier parts of the country. Buy budded trees on a tested rootstock from an accredited nursery, and keep out greening disease. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Land preparation for fruit trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is Okitsu (Satsuma mandarin) the same as Okitsu?
items.a: Yes. Okitsu (Satsuma mandarin) is another name for Okitsu, registered as NSIC 2005 Md 04. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.
The record shows a recorded yield of 10 kg/tree. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of Okitsu?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
